segments.title: Why outside pressure over Vietnam faced Cold War constraints
segments.body: Countries able to pressure the United States over Vietnam often had little incentive or room to act. The Soviet bloc was already in a nuclear standoff with Washington and traded little with it. American allies depended on US protection against that same threat. France's hostility to the Viet Cong also complicated the prospect of a common front against American policy.

evidence.note: Nuclear confrontation, limited trade, alliance dependence, and French hostility to the Viet Cong constrained outside pressure over Vietnam.

segments.summary: Nuclear confrontation, limited trade, and dependence on American protection restricted the countries that could pressure Washington over Vietnam.
segments.question: Which countries could realistically punish the United States over the Vietnam War?
segments.answerShort: Adversaries were already confronting Washington, while allies depended on American security; France also had its own hostility toward the Viet Cong.

segments.title: Why battleship spotting aircraft remained biplanes
segments.body: A gunfire-spotting aircraft has a different job from a reconnaissance aircraft. A battleship spotter needs to launch reliably, remain near the firing ship, and observe fall of shot. Greater speed adds little when the aircraft is flying repeated patterns over the fleet. Older aircraft technology could therefore remain well matched to this narrow naval mission.

evidence.note: Biplane lift and easy takeoff suited local gunfire spotting, where extra speed offered little benefit.

segments.summary: Biplanes remained useful as battleship spotting aircraft because lift and easy takeoff mattered more than the extra speed offered by a monoplane.
segments.question: Why was Britain slow to adopt monoplanes as battleship spotting aircraft?
segments.answerShort: Because biplanes offered strong lift and easy takeoff, while a monoplane's extra speed brought little benefit to an aircraft flying local spotting patterns rather than long-range reconnaissance.

segments.title: Paddle battleship: icebreaking, manoeuvre, and repair
segments.body: A wider bow could shield Icebreaker's side paddles in heavy ice, but the exposed arrangement serves other needs. The side paddles mainly provide manoeuvrability, while the stern paddle supplies speed. They can be raised or lowered for maintenance, and the fictional ship carries repair facilities. The arrangement sacrifices some icebreaking efficiency for ocean handling and access to damaged machinery. Its acceptability depends partly on being able to repair the paddles aboard.

evidence.note: Icebreaker's side paddles aid manoeuvring, its stern paddle provides speed, and lifting the paddles gives access for onboard repairs despite exposure in ice.

segments.summary: A paddle-wheel icebreaker battleship becomes a design exercise in balancing icebreaking efficiency against manoeuvrability, access for repairs, and ocean-going usefulness.

segments.title: OPEC and the risks of pressuring the United States
segments.body: Oil-exporting states had to balance American and Soviet influence. In the 1960s and 1970s, domestic instability and the possibility of a foreign-sponsored coup limited their freedom to confront either power. Any attempt to punish Washington therefore had to account for the security risks faced by the governments applying the pressure.

evidence.note: Oil-exporting governments balancing American and Soviet influence faced the danger of foreign-sponsored coups.

segments.summary: Oil-exporting states had to consider their own security and the danger of superpower intervention when weighing pressure over Vietnam.
segments.question: Could OPEC pressure the United States over Vietnam while relying on protection from communist uprisings?
segments.answerShort: Its members faced competing superpower pressures and the risk of American- or Soviet-sponsored coups, which complicated such a policy.

segments.title: How escorts reacted to the loss of HMS Hood
segments.body: Hood's escorts and Tribal-class destroyers were intensely angered by her sinking. The bond extended to ships that were not her sisters. Shared service with a lost vessel could give its consorts a strong desire for revenge.

evidence.note: Hood's escorts and Tribal-class destroyers provide an example of anger over the loss of a close consort.

segments.summary: Hood's escorts and Tribal-class destroyers illustrate how a lost consort could inspire a desire for revenge beyond a ship's own class.
segments.question: Did ships or intended sister ships ever seek revenge for a vessel that had been sunk?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Hood's escorts and Tribal-class destroyers were intensely angered by her loss, even though they were not her sister ships.

segments.title: Icebreaker's paddle wheels use biodiesel
segments.body: Icebreaker's paddle wheels do not establish that she is a steamship. The propulsion description is corrected to corn oil, identified as biodiesel. The visible paddle arrangement and the fuel used to power it are separate features of the design.

evidence.note: The steamer description is corrected to corn oil, explicitly identified as biodiesel.

segments.summary: The fictional paddle battleship runs on corn-oil biodiesel, despite the initial steamer label.

segments.title: Protecting the command successor and the tankers
segments.body: The lookout's greater height reveals approaching ships before Coral can see them from her own position. She insists on remaining where she can observe and command, while ordering O'Connor inside Icebreaker's armour. If she is hit, he must survive to take over. The squadron forms a declining echelon with the tankers furthest from the enemy. Command continuity and protection of support ships shape the formation before firing begins.

evidence.note: Lookout height affects sighting distance, O'Connor is ordered behind armour as Coral's successor, and the tankers take the protected side of the formation.

segments.summary: Coral keeps a successor behind Icebreaker's armour and places the tankers furthest from the approaching threat.

segments.title: Gunnery range, withheld intelligence, and the first shot
segments.body: Icebreaker's squadron makes 20 kilometres per hour while its pursuers travel at 30, closing the gap at 10 kilometres per hour and leaving time to assess the threat before Coral can see them from her position. Intelligence suggests that the opposing 20-centimetre guns elevate only to 20 degrees and reach about 20 kilometres, against 24 kilometres for Coral's guns. A history of bad intelligence has made the fictional navy reluctant to circulate reports before repeated confirmation. Its intelligence officer also has cases of paper and no support staff, prompting Coral to promise cleared yeomen. The apparent range advantage does not settle the political problem: firing first could begin the war the Republic is trying to avert. Yellow flares signal restraint while the squadron prepares for battle.

evidence.note: Closing speeds, differing gun elevations and ranges, delayed intelligence distribution, staffing shortages, and orders to signal restraint while preparing for battle.

segments.summary: Icebreaker's range advantage depends on intelligence that reached command late, while political restraint prevents Coral from simply firing first.

segments.title: Pennsylvania's crew after Arizona's loss
segments.body: Pennsylvania's crew probably carried a strong sense of grievance after Arizona's loss. Renown is suggested as another ship likely to feel that way about Hood. These are interpretations of crew sentiment, without a claim that revenge explains every later operation.

evidence.note: Probable revenge sentiment aboard Pennsylvania after Arizona's loss, with Renown offered as a parallel after Hood.

segments.summary: A desire for revenge is suggested as part of Pennsylvania's crew spirit after Arizona's destruction.
segments.question: How much did a desire to avenge Arizona affect Pennsylvania's crew in World War II?
segments.answerShort: Probably quite strongly at the level of crew spirit; Renown's feelings after Hood's loss are suggested as a similar case.

segments.title: Dual-purpose guns and the limits of improving ABDACOM
segments.body: Twin 4.7-inch dual-purpose weapons would make British and Australian ships more capable against air attack. The wider effect would depend on the composition of the force available to ABDACOM. Better guns alone do not establish how this counterfactual campaign would unfold.

evidence.note: Improved air-defence capability from 4.7-inch dual-purpose guns, with the overall force available to ABDACOM left as the decisive qualification.

segments.summary: Better dual-purpose guns would improve Allied air defence in the early Pacific war, but the effect still depends on the composition of the whole ABDACOM force.
segments.question: How would twin 4.7-inch dual-purpose guns on British and Australian ships affect the Pacific war and ABDACOM?
segments.answerShort: They would improve air-defence capability, but the wider effect depends heavily on what overall force ABDACOM has available.

segments.title: Why mechanical fire-control computers endured
segments.body: Mechanical fire-control tables remained useful into the 1960s. For large naval guns, they lasted longer because a replacement would require a new system designed from scratch. Funding that replacement was a separate obstacle from the ability to calculate a firing solution. This experience gives the Babbage-style naval computers in The Difference Engine a practical historical comparison.

evidence.note: Mechanical fire-control tables remained in use into the 1960s and longer for large guns, with replacement limited by the need to fund a new design.

segments.summary: The Difference Engine's mechanical fire-control premise is plausible because real mechanical fire-control tables remained effective for decades.
segments.question: What would limit a Babbage-style mechanical computer used for naval fire control?
segments.answerShort: Mechanical fire-control tables remained useful into the 1960s and lasted longer for large guns, where replacing them required a new system that nobody had funded.

segments.title: A stronger Britain and the strategic calculus of Vietnam
segments.body: A non-declining British Empire would still have to decide whether forcing the superpowers out of Vietnam served its interests. American and Soviet commitments there would absorb resources unavailable elsewhere. That could make continued involvement by both rivals advantageous to Britain. The calculation is explicitly condemned as cruel, even evil, while being treated as an incentive governments could act on.

evidence.note: The non-declining British Empire scenario raises a resource-diversion argument explicitly described as cruel and evil.

segments.summary: A stronger Britain could see an advantage in letting Vietnam absorb American and Soviet resources, despite the cruelty of that calculation.
segments.question: Would a non-declining British Empire force the United States and Soviet Union out of Vietnam?
segments.answerShort: It might prefer to let Vietnam absorb American and Soviet resources that would otherwise be available elsewhere.

segments.title: Environmental pressure and neglected naval force multipliers
segments.body: Icebreaker's environmental setting prompts a comparison with future wars shaped by environmental change. Large-scale, affordable desalination is one problem governments need to address, while the cost of applying available technology can delay other solutions. The naval parallel is Treasury pressure during the 1930s, when building sloops or fleet tankers could mean sacrificing destroyers or cruisers. Destroyers took priority because they were indispensable and could also perform much of a sloop's anti-submarine work. Sloops and Royal Fleet Auxiliary tankers nevertheless multiplied what the fleet could protect and sustain. Forcing support vessels to compete directly with major combatants could leave the fleet short of supporting capacity.

evidence.note: Cost can delay existing technical solutions, as illustrated by desalination and interwar choices between combatants, sloops, and fleet tankers.

segments.summary: Cost pressures can delay practical responses to environmental change, just as competition for naval funds can squeeze out sloops and tankers.

segments.title: Advanced fire control could bring the dreadnought idea forward
segments.body: Improved computation would let pre-dreadnought-era ships make practical use of their long-range guns. That capability could produce a vessel with a dreadnought-like gun arrangement during the 1890s, even if its machinery remained conventional. Effective fire control would change which armament layouts made sense. Propulsion was only one route toward the dreadnought concept.

evidence.note: Better long-range fire control could encourage a dreadnought-style gun layout in the 1890s without requiring the later propulsion system.

segments.summary: Giving 1890s fleets effective long-range fire control could encourage dreadnought-style armament while they retained older machinery.
segments.question: How would advanced mechanical fire control change fleets of the 1890s and early 1900s?
segments.answerShort: It would make long-range gunnery usable and could bring about a dreadnought-style gun layout in the 1890s, even without dreadnought-style machinery.

segments.title: Britain's alliance risks in the Vietnam counterfactual
segments.body: Trying to force an end to the conflict could risk Britain's American alliance. Confronting the Soviet Union directly would bring a different danger of war. Letting both powers spend resources in Vietnam could instead leave Britain with more influence elsewhere and across the Commonwealth. The harm to the Vietnamese people makes this calculation cruel despite its strategic attraction.

evidence.note: Britain's choices include risking the American alliance, confronting Russia, or allowing rivals to expend resources in Vietnam while gaining influence elsewhere.

segments.summary: A stronger Britain would weigh the cost of breaking with Washington or confronting Moscow against greater freedom elsewhere.
segments.question: Would the British Empire be better off letting the two sides continue fighting in Vietnam?
segments.answerShort: In that counterfactual, it could choose this cruel option to preserve the US alliance, avoid war with the Soviet Union, and gain freedom of action elsewhere.

segments.title: American oil production and Canadian imports
segments.body: American domestic petroleum production limits dependence on other oil exporters in this argument. Canada is identified as the next major source of imports. An oil-pressure scenario therefore needs to account for these supplies before assuming that exporters elsewhere can dictate American policy.

evidence.note: American domestic oil production and imports from Canada are offered as limits on the influence of other petroleum exporters.

segments.summary: Domestic petroleum and Canadian supplies limit the oil-pressure argument in the Vietnam discussion.

segments.title: Port Stanley if von Spee arrived before Sturdee
segments.body: If the German squadron approached Port Stanley before Admiral Sturdee's force arrived, a British battleship in harbour could fire using spotting arrangements. Von Spee's ships lacked the means to see and answer a target hidden beyond the hill. Spee would probably withdraw rather than remain under unanswered fire. Sturdee would then have to refuel and begin a much less certain ocean pursuit.

evidence.note: A British battleship can fire from behind the hill at Port Stanley, while von Spee's inability to reply makes withdrawal and a later ocean search likely.

segments.summary: If von Spee reached Port Stanley first, shore-obscured British battleship fire would probably drive him away and turn the battle into an ocean search.
segments.question: What happens if von Spee reaches Port Stanley before Sturdee?
segments.answerShort: A battleship in harbour could engage over the hill while von Spee could not effectively reply, probably forcing him back to sea and turning Sturdee's operation into an ocean search.

segments.title: British and Commonwealth support for Vietnam peace efforts
segments.body: British and Commonwealth support for peace efforts was strongest when Washington supported them too. When the United States did not, public expressions of interest tended to stop short of creating serious difficulties for its policy. Public support for a settlement could therefore coexist with reluctance to challenge an ally.

evidence.note: British and Commonwealth advocacy of a peace settlement is assessed as stronger when it followed the American position.

segments.summary: British and Commonwealth support for a Vietnam peace settlement was closely conditioned by the American position in this assessment.

segments.title: When hardtack likely left Royal Navy rations
segments.body: Hardtack probably remained a major Royal Navy ration until around the 1900s. That date is a recollection that would need checking against the records. Changes in biscuit recipes also complicate deciding when the older ration disappeared.

evidence.note: The 1900s date is tentative, with changing biscuit recipes and the need for further checking left explicit.

segments.summary: Hardtack's disappearance as a major Royal Navy ration is tentatively placed around the 1900s, with changing recipes complicating the date.
segments.question: When did Royal Navy ships stop carrying hardtack as a major part of their rations?
segments.answerShort: Probably around the 1900s, though the date is given from memory and needs further verification.

segments.title: A 1940 war gives Britain an escort advantage
segments.body: A September 1940 outbreak could put roughly sixty additional British escorts into service. German submarine production under another year of peacetime conditions would not rise at the same rate, while British anti-submarine construction was already positioned to expand sharply. Mobilization timing would therefore change the balance between U-boats and the smaller ships needed to contain them. The estimate concerns a counterfactual year of continued peacetime production, rather than a claim about the historical force in September 1939.

evidence.note: The counterfactual estimate adds about sixty Royal Navy escorts by September 1940 while German submarine production remains constrained by peacetime conditions.

segments.summary: Delaying the outbreak of war by a year would enlarge Britain's anti-submarine escort force faster than Germany could enlarge its U-boat arm in peacetime.
segments.question: How would a September 1940 start to the Second World War affect the naval balance?
segments.answerShort: Britain could have roughly sixty more escorts in service, while German peacetime submarine production would grow much less, creating a major anti-submarine advantage for the Royal Navy.

segments.title: Geese and the limits of low-level flight training
segments.body: Clarke recalls a Canadian Air Force officer saying that they avoided low-level flying over large areas of Canada because of geese. When asked about the loss of training opportunities, the officer put pilot survival first.

evidence.note: Clarke recalls an unnamed Canadian Air Force officer linking restrictions on low-level flying to the danger posed by geese.

segments.summary: A Canadian Air Force officer's reported experience links restrictions on low-level flying to the danger geese pose to fast jets.

segments.title: Germany's submarine disadvantage in a 1938 war
segments.body: A war in 1938 would find German submarine production even lower than in the proposed 1940 outbreak. Britain would also lack the later escort programmes: designs existed, but the ships had not yet been ordered. Germany's still smaller submarine force would leave it at a disadvantage in an earlier war.

evidence.note: German submarine production in 1938 is judged even less adequate than in the delayed-war scenario, despite Britain's later escort designs not yet being ordered.

segments.summary: Germany's low submarine production weakens the case that fighting during the 1938 Munich crisis would have been advantageous.
segments.question: Was Hitler right that Germany should have gone to war during the Munich crisis in 1938?
segments.answerShort: No. German submarine production was even lower in 1938, despite Britain also lacking its later escort-building programmes.

segments.title: Hood's deferred fire-control modernization
segments.body: Hood carried only a basic radar fit in 1941. A planned refit would have brought better radar and fire-control equipment. Her existing fit reflected the timing of modernization and the work still intended for her.

evidence.note: Hood's basic radar fit and the better radar and fire-control equipment intended for her planned refit.

segments.summary: Hood's basic radar fit was intended to be replaced by better radar and fire-control equipment during a larger refit.
segments.question: Why was Hood's fire control considered outdated by 1941?
segments.answerShort: Hood had only basic radar and was awaiting a planned refit with better radar and fire-control equipment.

segments.title: Service identity as a military institution
segments.body: Some service members give those in the same navy, army, branch, or regiment a special insider status. In the British Army example, the regiment supplies that boundary. People outside it become those the institution protects. Coral's outlook in Icebreaker uses the same division between those who belong to the service and those who depend on it.

evidence.note: Coral's naval identity resembles service and regimental attitudes that privilege uniformed insiders and view outsiders as people to protect.

segments.summary: A fictional admiral's worldview illustrates how service and regimental identity can divide insiders from the civilians they protect.

segments.title: Why British carrier construction mattered
segments.body: Uninterrupted construction would have accelerated British carrier output. The proposed priority is to pause battleships while keeping carriers and escorts under construction. Carriers supported counter-raider operations, anti-submarine warfare, fleet air defence, and deterrence in the Far East. A smoother handover from Henderson to Fraser could have preserved stronger advocacy for the carrier programme. Henderson's illness removed the senior figure considered best placed to challenge a pause, although others continued making the case.

evidence.note: Carrier missions, the proposed priority over battleship construction, and the effect of Henderson's illness and Fraser's handover on advocacy for the programme.

segments.summary: Keeping carriers under construction while pausing battleships could preserve the ships required for several British naval missions.
segments.question: How much would British battleship and carrier production have accelerated without the construction pause for escorts?
segments.answerShort: Dramatically, although the proposed priority is to keep carriers under construction and pause battleships first.

segments.title: Admiralty and Dreyer fire-control tables
segments.body: The tentative distinction is improved accuracy and the ability to incorporate more data. A detailed account of how the two tables differ would require closer examination of their machinery.

evidence.note: Provisional comparison based on accuracy and the range of data inputs, with further examination needed.

segments.summary: The Admiralty Fire Control Table is tentatively distinguished by greater accuracy and more data inputs.
segments.question: What was the difference between the Admiralty Fire Control Table and the Dreyer table?
segments.answerShort: Tentatively, improved accuracy and more data inputs; the technical comparison remains provisional.

segments.title: Czech defences and industry in a 1938 war
segments.body: Czechoslovakia's border mountains, forts, artillery, and tanks would make a 1938 German attack costly. Poland would have an opportunity to mobilize, and France could advance while the German Army was less developed than it became in 1939. Germany would also lack access to Czech factories and military facilities. Those resources mattered to its later preparations, so an earlier war would change both the initial fighting and Germany's industrial position.

evidence.note: Fortified Czech terrain, Polish mobilization, possible French action, and German dependence on Czech industrial resources in the 1938 counterfactual.

segments.summary: A 1938 war would confront Germany with fortified Czech mountain borders while denying it the factories acquired after Munich.

segments.title: The arithmetic behind King George V's 14-inch guns
segments.body: Britain's choice of 14-inch weapons partly reflected a desire to demonstrate political leadership while European rivals announced 15-inch ships. The naval argument depended on fitting twelve 14-inch guns, whose greater number of shells could plausibly compete with eight 15-inch weapons. Once the design fell to ten 14-inch guns, that volume-of-fire advantage became much less convincing against eight or nine larger guns. The diplomatic case and the original armament arithmetic both shaped the decision.

evidence.note: Political leadership and a proposed twelve-gun 14-inch battery support the original choice, while reducing it to ten guns weakens the comparison with eight or nine 15-inch weapons.

segments.summary: Britain's 14-inch choice could be defended politically and by a planned twelve-gun broadside, but the case weakened when the finished design carried only ten guns.
segments.question: Why did Britain choose 14-inch guns in 1936 when European powers were announcing 15-inch battleships?
segments.answerShort: Political leadership mattered, and a planned twelve-gun 14-inch battery promised a strong volume of fire; the logic became weaker when the ship ended up with ten guns.

segments.title: Strategy can mean avoiding a catastrophic defeat
segments.body: The desire to win a battle differs from the need to avoid losing one, especially when war appears deceptively binary. Nuclear escalation shows how a tactical result can create a worse strategic position by devastating a country, driving wider proliferation, and giving enemies strong reasons for revenge. A nominal victory could leave the victor with an unmanageable political and human aftermath. The surrounding fictional campaign uses this distinction to judge risk and restraint.

evidence.note: Nuclear escalation could create diplomatic isolation, wider proliferation, destruction, and demands for revenge even after an apparent military victory.

segments.summary: A tactical victory can still leave a worse strategic position through destruction, proliferation, and lasting hostility.

segments.title: Fighter screens, missile reserves, and delayed sensor reports
segments.body: In Stand Defiant, Walking Stick keeps his starfighters roughly a light-second ahead of the main fleet to screen incoming missiles without committing them to a separate fighter battle. A victory in that duel would still cost fighters he does not need to lose. Clearing orbital mines has depleted his missile stocks, leaving too few for speculative shots at extreme range. Wider sensor-drone spacing could reveal what the opposing fleet is hiding, but the drones no longer have their instantaneous quantum links. With the fleets still 97 million kilometres apart, he accepts another five seconds of reporting delay to obtain a broader view.

evidence.note: Forward fighter screening, conservation of fighters and scarce missiles, and wider sensor coverage at the cost of light-speed reporting delay in Stand Defiant.

segments.summary: Stand Defiant links the placement of a fighter screen to missile shortages and delays in reports from widely spread sensor drones.

segments.title: Deception can make victory unaffordable
segments.body: An apparent second fleet turns a favourable engagement against fifteen ships into a much less certain battle. Jamming and decoys prevent Walking Stick from establishing how many reinforcements are real or whether they belong to mercenaries or a hostile state. Identifiable starfighters establish that some of the new force is genuine, while leaving its full strength unresolved. He might still win, but the resulting losses could endanger the Commonwealth. He withdraws because the wider war requires the fleet to survive. His characteristic error in this interpretation of the fictional commander is overconfidence in his ability to manage capable opponents.

evidence.note: Uncertain reinforcements, fighter identification, competing explanations for the new force, and withdrawal to preserve the Commonwealth's fleet.

segments.summary: Uncertain reinforcements make a likely tactical victory too costly for a fictional commander whose fleet must survive the wider war.

segments.title: An interwar naval race would reward quality over numbers
segments.body: Britain would continue building battleships if other powers did so. The Anglo-German contest before World War I was an explicitly numerical competition. A 1920s race with the United States and Japan is expected to concentrate more on technology and the size and quality of individual ships. In that counterfactual, Britain would probably build four G3 battlecruisers and four N3 battleships.

evidence.note: A postwar British-American-Japanese technology race is contrasted with the earlier numerical rivalry with Germany, with four G3s and four N3s suggested for Britain.

segments.summary: Without effective naval treaties, Britain would still answer American and Japanese battleship construction, but the contest would likely emphasize the largest and best ships rather than German-style numerical parity.
segments.question: Would postwar conditions have prevented Britain from joining another battleship race if naval treaties failed?
segments.answerShort: No. Britain would build if the United States and Japan did, but the race would probably emphasize ship quality and size rather than the numerical rivalry seen against Germany.

segments.title: Why Hood and Rodney received the Dreyer Mk V table
segments.body: Commissioning and upgrade dates shaped which fire-control equipment Hood and Rodney received.

evidence.note: Service-entry and upgrade timing as the explanation for the Dreyer Mk V installations on Hood and Rodney.

segments.summary: The Dreyer Mk V fit on Hood and Rodney is linked to commissioning and upgrade dates.
segments.question: Why were Hood and Rodney the only ships to receive the Dreyer Fire Control Table Mk V?
segments.answerShort: The fit reflected when the ships entered service and when they were upgraded.

segments.title: Hood's four-inch battery and weight limits
segments.body: Two tentative solutions are proposed for the four-inch battery. Hood could be fitted for weapons that were not all installed, or weight could be saved elsewhere to accommodate them. Neither option is presented as a confirmed account of what the Royal Navy did.

evidence.note: Tentative alternatives of fitting for but not with the guns or finding weight savings elsewhere.

segments.summary: Hood's weight problem could require gun positions prepared for later installation or compensating weight reductions elsewhere.
segments.question: How could the Royal Navy accommodate Hood's four-inch guns if their weight was a problem?
segments.answerShort: Possible solutions were to prepare positions without installing every gun or to remove weight elsewhere.

segments.title: Strategic intelligence means deciding with an incomplete picture
segments.body: Neither commander possesses a complete picture. Strategic intelligence must combine events across an entire system with knowledge of the opponent, the intentions of third parties, and the limitations of one's own fleet. Walking Stick has concentrated everything he has, leaving no reserve to absorb losses or answer the next threat. Under those conditions, even a likely tactical victory can be strategically unacceptable.

evidence.note: Incomplete battlefield and strategic intelligence, other factions, knowledge of the opposing commander, and Walking Stick's lack of a reserve constrain his choices.

segments.summary: The battle in Stand Defiant combines incomplete battlefield information with knowledge of other powers and the limits of a fleet that has no reserve behind it.

segments.title: Why Britain occupied Iceland in 1940
segments.body: A small German landing could create a strategic crisis without a large amphibious invasion. A reinforced battalion concealed aboard a merchant ship might seize an island without armed forces of its own, with further troops potentially arriving by air. German-held Iceland could provide an aircraft base threatening North Atlantic convoys. Retaking it would require a difficult British amphibious operation and expose Icelandic civilians to fighting. Preemptive British occupation denied Germany that opportunity, and American troops later took over the garrison responsibility.

evidence.note: A hypothetical small German landing, Iceland's potential as an Atlantic air base, the danger and cost of recapture, and the subsequent American garrison.
German occupation would require a greater British commitment and expose Icelandic civilians to fighting during recapture.

segments.summary: Britain occupied Iceland to prevent a small German seizure from creating an air and naval base that would endanger Atlantic convoys and require a costly amphibious recovery.

segments.title: Graf Zeppelin could force a North Atlantic carrier hunt
segments.body: A completed Graf Zeppelin would present Britain with a serious counterfactual problem because even an inefficient carrier would enlarge a German task force's options. The Royal Navy might have to concentrate Furious, Ark Royal, and, depending on timing, Victorious to find and defeat it. A fast capital ship would likely accompany those carriers against the German surface force. One carrier would therefore change the force required to contain the entire raider group.

evidence.note: A hypothetical Graf Zeppelin task force and the possible British response using Furious, Ark Royal, Victorious, and a fast capital ship.

segments.summary: A completed Graf Zeppelin could make a German Atlantic task force dangerous enough to draw several British carriers and a fast capital ship into a dedicated hunt.

segments.title: Fire-control backups from duplicate tables to local control
segments.body: Ships could duplicate fire-control tables and positions where space allowed. On a smaller ship, destruction of a well-protected table could mean the vessel already had much more serious damage. At short ranges, guns could use local control without the full long-range calculation system. HMS Exeter's gunnery officer directed a gun from atop its turret, observing fall of shot and shouting corrections.

evidence.note: Duplicate tables and control positions, close-range local control, and Exeter's gunnery officer directing fire from a turret.

segments.summary: Duplicate fire-control positions and local gun control offered alternatives when a warship's main system failed.
segments.question: What backup existed if a warship's main fire-control system failed?
segments.answerShort: Ships could use duplicate tables and control positions or shift to local control at shorter range, with officers observing fall of shot and directing corrections.

segments.title: How a German attack on Ireland could aid Atlantic convoys
segments.body: German troops would have to cross British airspace or take a long route around Britain to reach Ireland. Survivors would face Irish armed forces and veterans who had fought Germany in World War I. Reinforcing an isolated landing would create another serious problem. An attack could turn Ireland into Germany's enemy and give Britain access to Irish airfields and convoy assembly areas.

evidence.note: Difficult flight routes and reinforcement, Irish resistance, and the possibility that an attack would open Irish airfields and convoy assembly areas to Britain.

segments.summary: A German airborne attack on Ireland would be hard to sustain and could push Ireland into the Allied camp, opening valuable Atlantic bases for convoy and anti-submarine operations.
segments.question: What would happen if Germany attempted an airborne attack on Ireland?
segments.answerShort: The force would be difficult to deliver and reinforce, while the attack could bring Ireland into the war and open its airfields and Atlantic ports to Allied convoy and anti-submarine forces.

segments.title: Why gunnery officers needed to check the tables
segments.body: Well-trained gunnery officers could make calculations themselves and challenge incorrect results from a table. A computer operator likewise needs an independent idea of what the answer should be. Knowing the underlying method allows a check that the output is in the right range. A calculating aid is harder to trust when nobody can recognize a bad result.

evidence.note: Manual calculation and practical understanding as checks on a table or computer's output.

segments.summary: Officers needed enough practical knowledge to recognize when a fire-control table or computer was giving an implausible result.

segments.title: Plan Kathleen and the absence of Irish government support
segments.body: Plan Kathleen is assessed as an unpromising scheme for taking Northern Ireland. The Irish government was not involved. Cooperation with Nazi Germany would have put the IRA in considerable difficulty, a danger that some of its members recognized.

evidence.note: Lack of Irish government participation and the anticipated difficulties of IRA cooperation with Nazi Germany.

segments.summary: Plan Kathleen lacked Irish government involvement, while cooperation with Nazi Germany offered the IRA a hazardous course.

segments.title: Irish convoy assembly and forward escort bases
segments.body: The Irish Sea is less calm than Halifax, but a convoy could assemble there while already under steam. In a sufficiently secure area, ships could join the formation and build up speed before leaving. Access to Irish harbours would also allow escorts and hunter-killer groups to operate from positions closer to Atlantic convoys. These advantages depend on the counterfactual in which a German attack brings Ireland into the war.

evidence.note: Convoy assembly under steam in a secured Irish Sea despite less sheltered conditions than Halifax.
Irish harbours as forward bases for escorts and hunter-killer groups in the German-invasion counterfactual.

segments.summary: Irish access could permit convoys to assemble while underway and place escort groups closer to their Atlantic operating areas.

segments.title: North Carolina Scheme XVI or King George V?
segments.body: The choice concerns the designs before the escalator clause. Neither proposal is favoured: the King George V design is disliked, and the corresponding North Carolina design is unappealing too. This is a personal design preference without a detailed technical ranking.

evidence.note: Explicit personal dislike of both King George V and the pre-escalator North Carolina design, without a technical comparison.

segments.summary: A comparison of North Carolina Scheme XVI and King George V ends with a personal preference for neither design.
segments.question: Which was the better battleship design without the escalator clause: North Carolina Scheme XVI or King George V?
segments.answerShort: The personal preference is for neither design.

segments.title: Shared design faults and sister-ship modifications
segments.body: Closely spaced losses of ships in the same class are considered rarer than the aircraft accidents in the question's example. Sea conditions often contribute to a sinking, complicating an explanation based on design alone. When one ship reveals a problem staying afloat, the normal response is to modify the rest of the class to address it.

evidence.note: Rarity of closely spaced sister-ship losses, the influence of sea conditions, and modifications following a flotation problem.

segments.summary: A flotation problem in one ship normally prompts modifications to its sisters.
segments.question: Do ships suffer repeated losses from a shared design flaw in the way aircraft sometimes do?
segments.answerShort: Such closely spaced losses are considered rarer, and a flotation problem in one ship normally prompts modifications to its sisters.

segments.title: Matching velocity to intercept a missile swarm
segments.body: Five destroyers face about 15,000 incoming missiles with 56 launchers and roughly 3,400 defensive missiles between them. Their advantage is acceleration: they can move into a more favourable range and relative velocity than the planet's fixed defences. Once they match the swarm's speed, lasers and shields can supplement the counter-missiles, although incoming weapons with fuel remaining could still manoeuvre against them. The ammunition carried also limits their options. Converting ordinary nuclear warheads into directional warheads would take days, while the interception is only hours away. These constraints belong to the fictional battle, where acceleration, weapon stocks, and preparation time determine the available defence.

evidence.note: Five destroyers seek a favourable intercept against roughly 15,000 missiles, with 56 launchers, about 3,400 missiles, lasers, and shields.
Available warhead types constrain the defence because conversion work would require days and contact is only hours away.

segments.summary: Five fictional destroyers must match a missile swarm's velocity before their limited counter-missiles, lasers, and shields can protect a planet.

segments.title: How a blocking escort force defeats stealth raiders
segments.body: Thirty stealth raiders threaten fighters pursuing the defeated fleet. Twenty allied escorts block their attack, despite being outnumbered. The raiders are only about a third of the escorts' size and depend on surprise and single-shot launchers. Once their attack exposes them to the blocking force, those limitations leave them unable to win the engagement.

evidence.note: Thirty small stealth raiders encounter twenty larger escorts after turning to attack fighters, losing the surprise on which their single-shot weapons depend.

segments.summary: Fictional stealth raiders lose their advantage when attacking fighters brings them within reach of a prepared escort squadron.

segments.title: Samar and the destroyer's duty to protect others
segments.body: The destroyer crews compare their predicament with the Battle off Samar and Sprague's defence of the escort carriers. Their captain points out that Sprague had more ships and carriers, while their own immediate responsibility is a civilian population. In the fictional navy, Samar and the Atlantic convoy battles form part of a destroyer officer's education. The principle drawn from them is that warships must stand between those they protect and an attacker. Victory elsewhere has left the surviving main fleet badly placed to stop the incoming strike, so the smaller screening force still has a separate battle to fight.

evidence.note: The fictional crews invoke Sprague, Samar, and Atlantic convoy warfare while preparing to defend civilians with the main fleet out of position.

segments.summary: The Battle off Samar supplies a historical model for fictional destroyers protecting civilians while the main fleet is out of position.

segments.title: Jamming and command delay in missile defence
segments.body: The destroyers launch 112 missiles per minute, but their stock is too small to stop the attack through one-for-one interceptions. Enemy jammer missiles activate in successive groups timed to interfere with each defensive salvo. The interceptors are nearly two light-seconds away, leaving a four-second command-and-control loop that is too slow to rescue the first disrupted attack. Jamming also makes it difficult to assess how many incoming weapons have been destroyed. Even missiles carrying jammers remain dangerous because their high velocity makes them destructive projectiles without nuclear warheads. The defenders must destroy or deflect those missiles too.

evidence.note: Repeated jammer activations disrupt counter-missile targeting, a four-second command loop prevents timely correction, and jammer missiles remain dangerous kinetic threats.

segments.summary: Successive jammer bursts disrupt a fictional missile screen while a four-second command loop prevents timely targeting corrections.

segments.title: Launcher endurance and safe interception courses
segments.body: The destroyers carry enough ammunition for thirty minutes of sustained fire, but their launchers were designed to expend it over several engagements. Continuous firing every thirty seconds begins breaking the launchers before the magazines are empty. With missile interception proving insufficient, the ships prepare to sweep through the remaining weapons with their shields. Each course must miss the planet even if a destroyer loses engine power. Otherwise, a ship defending the population could itself become a catastrophic projectile.

evidence.note: Continuous firing causes launcher failures aboard Paladin and other destroyers, forcing shield sweeps on trajectories that miss the planet even after propulsion failure.

segments.summary: Sustained fire damages a fictional squadron's launchers, forcing shield sweeps on courses that remain safe after propulsion failure.

segments.title: Regimental identity in the 4th Royal Tank Regiment
segments.body: Stuart Crawford's Tank Commander is a personal history of British armoured service from the Cold War through the 1991 Gulf War and beyond. The 4th Royal Tank Regiment recruited heavily in Scotland and regarded itself as distinct from the other Royal Tank Regiment units. Crawford thought its proportion of Scots might exceed that of any Scottish regiment, while acknowledging that he could not prove the claim. Its pipes and drums had been established in the mid-1970s despite institutional disapproval. Rivalry with sister regiments coexisted with friendships formed on courses, contacts with cavalry regiments, and a close affinity with the Royal Scots Dragoon Guards. Crawford regretted the rejection of a proposed amalgamation with that regiment, whose recruiting area matched the 4th's. Instead, the 4th and 1st Royal Tank Regiments merged in 1993.

evidence.note: Crawford's recollections cover Scottish regimental identity, the unproved comparison with other Scottish units, resistance to pipes and drums, cavalry friendships, and disappointment over amalgamation.

segments.summary: Stuart Crawford recalls the 4th Royal Tank Regiment's Scottish identity, relations with other armoured regiments, and disappointment over its eventual amalgamation.

segments.title: Why science fiction calls so many warships cruisers
segments.body: Cruiser historically described a cruising role as well as a broad category below capital ships. That flexibility gives a fictional fleet room for vessels with different missions under the same general label. A designer can use cruiser for a large non-capital combatant without matching one precise historical type. The multiplayer game Dreadnought provides an example with its artillery cruiser terminology.

evidence.note: Cruiser combines a historical role with a broad non-capital ship category, giving fictional designers a flexible label.

segments.summary: Science fiction borrows the word cruiser because historically it described a flexible cruising role as well as a broad place below capital ships in the fleet hierarchy.
segments.question: Why do science-fiction games use so many different types of vessel called cruisers?
segments.answerShort: Because cruiser historically described a broad cruising role as much as a fixed size, making it a flexible label for the largest non-capital surface combatants in a fictional fleet.

segments.title: Treaty loopholes and a giant pre-dreadnought
segments.body: If treaty limits applied specifically to dreadnoughts, a mixed-battery pre-dreadnought could fall outside them. The proposed ship grows beyond 30,000 tons while preserving the older division between main and secondary armament. Four 18-inch guns provide the main battery, with 16-inch guns in wing turrets as secondaries. A Lord Nelson-style arrangement could give a broadside of four guns of each calibre. Its size and complexity follow from exploiting the classification used by the hypothetical treaty.

evidence.note: A hypothetical exemption for pre-dreadnoughts permits a mixed-battery design of 30,000 tons or more.
Four 18-inch main guns and 16-inch wing-turret secondaries provide a broadside of four guns of each calibre.

segments.summary: A hypothetical treaty exemption for pre-dreadnoughts could produce a ship of more than 30,000 tons with four 18-inch guns and 16-inch wing-turret secondaries.
segments.question: What unusual warship would you design if a treaty loophole allowed it?
segments.answerShort: A very large pre-dreadnought could exploit an exemption from dreadnought limits, using four 18-inch main guns and 16-inch wing-turret secondaries to retain a mixed battery.

segments.title: Why US troops could remain in a British-defended Europe
segments.body: Even if a stronger Britain could meet Europe's military needs, American troops would still have a political purpose there. Shared deployment would bind Anglo-American commitments against a third power. The same reasoning applies to the American desire for British and French forces in Germany. Joining military commitments helps bring the participating states' foreign policies together.

evidence.note: American troops in Europe would bind Anglo-American commitments, just as British and French deployments in Germany helped align Western foreign policies.

segments.summary: Even if a stronger Britain could cover European defence, American troops would still bind US and British policy together and demonstrate a shared commitment against another power.
segments.question: Would the United States still station troops in Europe if a stronger Britain could defend it?
segments.answerShort: Yes; the deployment would help bind Anglo-American strategy and foreign policy together, beyond the number of troops strictly needed for defence.

segments.title: War suits and the composition of a combat patrol
segments.body: A lone Invictor tactical war suit is an unappealing choice for this proposed Warhammer force. The preferred arrangement would deploy a squadron of war suits together and alongside dreadnoughts. A combat patrol would instead receive an armoured vehicle. This personal approach to composing a fictional force assigns equipment according to its intended role and supporting units.

evidence.note: A personal force-composition preference favours war suits in squadrons alongside dreadnoughts, while assigning an armoured vehicle to a combat patrol.

segments.summary: A fictional combat patrol raises a force-composition question: whether to field one war suit, a coordinated group, or an armoured vehicle.

segments.title: Fisher's Dreadnought and the value of gun volume
segments.body: Single 16-inch turrets would not provide the volume of fire Fisher wanted for HMS Dreadnought at long range. Elswick had repeatedly tried to sell Britain a 14-inch gun for its battleships. Had Britain adopted that weapon for the Lord Nelson class, Dreadnought could plausibly have followed with twin 14-inch turrets. The proposal links gun calibre to the number of guns available for long-range fire.

evidence.note: Fisher's desired volume of long-range fire favours twin 14-inch turrets over single 16-inch mounts, with prior Lord Nelson adoption providing the proposed route.

segments.summary: Fisher's preference for enough guns to sustain long-range fire makes twin 14-inch turrets more plausible than single 16-inch mounts in this counterfactual.
segments.question: Would Fisher have built HMS Dreadnought with single 16-inch turrets?
segments.answerShort: No. Single 16-inch mounts lack the long-range volume of fire Fisher wanted; an earlier adoption of 14-inch guns could instead have led to twin 14-inch mounts.

segments.title: French battleships if Italy stays outside the naval treaty
segments.body: Italy remaining outside the naval treaty is the proposed change that would permit France to obtain its Normandie- and Lyon-class battleships.

evidence.note: Italy staying outside the naval treaty is offered in answer to a question about French Normandie and Lyon battleships.

segments.summary: Keeping Italy outside the naval treaty is proposed as the route to French Normandie and Lyon battleships.
segments.question: How could France obtain its Normandie and Lyon battleships in an alternate history?
segments.answerShort: Have Italy stay outside the naval treaty.

segments.title: Heavy gunships, cruisers, and fictional fleet choices
segments.body: The gunship is treated as the larger option, while the cruiser is preferred for flexibility. Balanced task groups are the usual preference, but all-Battlestar fleets are also used in Battlestar Galactica: Deadlock. These are personal game choices rather than fixed definitions for real gunships and cruisers.

evidence.note: The heavy gunship is identified as larger, the cruiser is preferred for flexibility, and an all-Battlestar fleet is acknowledged as a personal game choice.

segments.summary: The heavy gunship is the larger option; cruiser flexibility suits the preferred style of play.
segments.question: How might a heavy gunship differ from a heavy cruiser in a science-fiction game?
segments.answerShort: The gunship is bigger; the cruiser is the preferred choice for flexibility.

segments.title: How a 14-inch Dreadnought could accelerate gun escalation
segments.body: A Dreadnought starting with 14-inch guns would leave later British classes needing a larger step in armament. The Orion class, which historically moved to 13.5-inch guns, would need a different improvement, with 16-inch guns emerging as a possibility. That would put further pressure on the Queen Elizabeth class to carry larger guns or triple 16-inch turrets. These are proposed consequences of the counterfactual, with no single later calibre treated as inevitable.

evidence.note: A hypothetical 14-inch Dreadnought leads to possible 16-inch Orions and Queen Elizabeth designs with larger guns or triple 16-inch turrets.

segments.summary: Beginning HMS Dreadnought with 14-inch guns could force later British classes toward 16-inch weapons, triple turrets, or still larger calibres much earlier.
segments.question: What follows if HMS Dreadnought begins with twin 14-inch guns?
segments.answerShort: Later classes would need to escalate sooner, potentially moving the Orions toward 16-inch guns and forcing the Queen Elizabeth class toward triple 16-inch mounts or 17- to 18-inch weapons.

segments.title: Mutually supporting Battlestar groups
segments.body: Jamie stacks ships in Battlestar Galactica: Deadlock, while Clarke finds that arrangement difficult to manoeuvre. The preferred alternative is separated groups of three that can support one another. Smaller Battlestars escort larger vessels, with one assigned a defensive role and another contributing additional strike elements. Strike fighters add to the formation's offensive strength.

evidence.note: Clarke prefers separated groups of three, while Jamie uses stacking; smaller Battlestars provide defensive cover and additional strike elements.

segments.summary: In Battlestar Galactica: Deadlock, mutually supporting groups of three let smaller Battlestars screen larger ships while adding strike capacity.
segments.question: Do you stack Battlestars together in Battlestar Galactica: Deadlock?
segments.answerShort: Stacking has been tried, but groups of three are preferred because they are easier to manoeuvre and can support one another.

segments.title: Allied unity and an American us-or-them outlook
segments.body: Visible allied unity fitted an American us-or-them view of the Cold War. The paranoia associated with that outlook helped Senator McCarthy rise to prominence. Clarke recalls relatives who lived in the United States at the time and returned to Britain with an unfavourable impression.

evidence.note: Public allied unity is connected to an us-or-them outlook, McCarthy-era paranoia, and Clarke's recollection of relatives returning from the United States.

segments.summary: An us-or-them view of the Cold War helps explain the importance attached to public allied unity despite criticism of American conduct.
segments.question: Why was a show of allied unity so important to the United States despite criticism of its conduct in the 1960s?
segments.answerShort: An us-or-them outlook made solidarity important, with anti-communist paranoia and the rise of McCarthyism offered as an explanation.

segments.title: A December 2022 operational pause: training and logistics
segments.body: In this assessment from December 2022, the Russo-Ukrainian War had reached a pause after recent advances. Russian conscripts still needed training and equipment, while the Ukrainian advance had stretched its logistics. These limits were expected to slow movement by both sides. Dramatic claims of success during the pause warranted caution because propaganda would continue even without major operational gains.

evidence.note: A December 2022 assessment attributes limited movement to Russian training and equipment needs and stretched Ukrainian logistics, while warning about competing propaganda claims.

segments.summary: A December 2022 assessment describes a temporary operational pause while Russia trained and equipped conscripts and Ukrainian logistics were stretched after an advance.

segments.title: Small Battlestars as escorts
segments.body: The smaller Battlestars are useful as escorts for the larger vessels. Their role is to support the formation around those ships.

evidence.note: Small Battlestars are recommended as escorts for larger Battlestars.

segments.summary: Small Battlestars earn their place by escorting larger ships in Battlestar Galactica: Deadlock.
segments.question: What are small Battlestars good for?
segments.answerShort: They escort the larger Battlestars.

segments.title: Chieftain performance depended on maintenance
segments.body: A viewer remembers the Chieftain as a comfortable pillbox. When working properly and well maintained, it was excellent. Its road and obstacle clearance let it cross a wide range of obstacles.

evidence.note: Chieftain performance qualified by working condition and maintenance, especially its road and obstacle clearance.

segments.summary: A Chieftain in working order and properly maintained offered excellent road and obstacle clearance.
segments.question: Was the Chieftain effective despite its problems?
segments.answerShort: When working properly and well maintained, it was excellent, especially for its road and obstacle clearance.

segments.title: A Victorian rail link and wartime supply
segments.body: The proposed Victorian rail link appears to be a Channel Tunnel, although the surviving question does not name it. Brunel is apparently the engineer intended in the reply, which stresses difficult construction, high cost, and loss of life. Broad gauge is suggested. In World War I the link would make supplying the Western Front much easier. In World War II the army could fall back toward it, although the link would probably be blown up.

evidence.note: A partially preserved question about a proposed link leads to Victorian construction under an apparently intended Brunel, broad gauge, easier Western Front supply, and a World War II withdrawal route with probable destruction.

segments.summary: A proposed Victorian rail link could ease Western Front supply in World War I and become a withdrawal route in World War II, when its destruction is considered likely.
segments.question: How early could the proposed rail link be built, and what would it change in the world wars?
segments.answerShort: A Victorian project is considered possible despite its cost and danger; it could simplify Western Front supply and later serve as a withdrawal route before being destroyed.

segments.title: Why large space warships may combine several roles
segments.body: A Battlestar combines roles associated with battleships, carriers, and assault ships. That mixture could suit large spacecraft. A ship arriving at its destination needs the ability to handle whatever work awaits it. The Daedalus class provides another fictional example of the preference for a versatile ship.

evidence.note: Battlestars' mixed roles as a plausible arrangement for large space warships, with the Daedalus class as another favoured design.

segments.summary: Large space warships may need battleship, carrier, and assault-ship capabilities because they must arrive able to handle varied demands.
segments.question: Are Battlestars incoherent because they combine battleship, carrier, and assault-ship roles?
segments.answerShort: Large space warships may need to perform several jobs, making a combination of battleship, carrier, and assault-ship roles plausible.

segments.title: Navigation lights in a blacked-out convoy
segments.body: Wartime ships could be completely blacked out, including their navigation lights. Convoys also had to keep ships from colliding as they moved together. Very dim navigation lights were therefore retained when required, and crews tried to keep them working. Their practical purpose was to help ships avoid one another.

evidence.note: Complete blackout is contrasted with very dim convoy navigation lights used to help ships avoid one another.

segments.summary: Wartime ships could run completely dark, but convoys often retained extremely dim navigation lights to reduce the danger of colliding with one another.
segments.question: What was the wartime protocol for navigation lights on merchant ships?
segments.answerShort: Ships could be completely blacked out, but convoys generally tried to retain very dim navigation lights so vessels could avoid colliding with one another.

segments.title: The limits of an American embargo against allies
segments.body: A blockade is considered unlikely in this hypothetical dispute with allies active against communism in the Caribbean. An embargo remains a possibility. Goods moving across the Atlantic and back would make such restrictions harder to enforce. The particular countries and measures are unspecified in the surviving question.

evidence.note: A question about anti-communist allies in the Caribbean receives a distinction between an unlikely blockade and a possible embargo complicated by Atlantic trade.

segments.summary: A hypothetical US blockade against allies opposing communism in the Caribbean is doubted, while an embargo remains possible but difficult to enforce through Atlantic trade.
segments.question: Would the United States embargo allies who were preventing communism from gaining a foothold in the Caribbean?
segments.answerShort: An actual blockade is considered unlikely; an embargo remains possible, although trade across the Atlantic and back would complicate it.

segments.title: Choosing wargames to support historical research
segments.body: Wargaming can serve as an aid to research. The choice of system depends on what needs to be investigated or worked out. Harpoon is one of several games used for that purpose.

evidence.note: Wargaming as a research aid, with the choice of game depending on the problem and Harpoon among the systems used.

segments.summary: The research question determines which wargame is useful, with Harpoon among the systems used.
segments.question: How useful is wargaming as an aid to research, and which games suit the work?
segments.answerShort: Wargaming is useful as a research aid, and the choice of game depends on the problem being examined; Harpoon is one example.
